event: Nala says: "Hi there, would you mind pointing me in the direction of your parents?"
The boy's face splits in a grin. "Pointing? I'll take you. My da's the reeve of Harrow, he is."
He swings the switch and turns the whole flock back east, geese squawking at the change.
"I'm Hob. Da's Aldous Crane. He keeps the roll. Everyone has to answer to him."
He doesn't wait for her name; he's onto the dogs, all howling at once round three o'clock.
"And the air hummed, like bees in a wall. And all the crows went up off the Mile at once."
"Mam says it's nothing. Da went quiet, which means it's something."
The road runs down into the village; the sun slips under the rise and the light goes grey-gold.
Hob steers the geese round the back of a long thatched alehouse with a sheaf painted on its sign.
Mutton stew smells through its back shutters; he pens the geese in a wattle fold, talking all along.
Then out onto the green: a well, a tall bell post, cottages of daub and thatch all round.
An old woman sits by her door shelling beans into her lap; she squints their way and sees little.
A man at a gate stops with a bucket; two women in a doorway lean their heads together.
Nala's bare feet go quiet on the grass of the green; every eye on it follows her.
Hob marches her to a house on the green's east side, stone-footed, by the bell post.
He bangs the door with the switch. "Da! I found a lady on the road! She's got no shoes!"
The door opens: a lean man of fifty, grey at the temples, napkin in hand, supper behind him.
He looks at her face and goes still, the napkin halfway to the table.
Something crosses his face, fast; he looks harder, then at the dusk behind her, then back.
Behind him a stout woman with a ladle peers past his shoulder, frowning at Nala's bare feet.
The man speaks slow and careful. "Evening, mistress."
"Your name, if you'd give it. Where's your home, and what's your business in Harrow?"
